title: Psychiatric CNVs: Schizophrenia Hot Spots, Bipolar Loci and Autism Heritability
summary: Learn what copy number variants and chromosomal microarray can and cannot show, the eight genome-wide schizophrenia CNV loci and how bipolar disorder differs, and the heritability and prevalence figures for bipolar disorder and autism.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 73 Hits 4 (schizophrenia CNV hot spots), 10 (bipolar prevalence, heritability, CNVs) and 12 (autism prevalence and heritability) and Trap 3 (CNV burden differs between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder). Checked against Marshall 2017 (abstract via Europe PMC; results read via a page-fetch tool), Green 2016, Kerner 2014, Merikangas 2011 (abstract), Bai 2019 (abstract), Maenner 2023 and Miller 2010 (abstract). Qualifications recorded as register flags: CNV direction for the schizophrenia loci (rv-ch73-scz-cnv-direction), only 16p11.2 surviving correction in bipolar disorder (rv-ch73-bipolar-cnv-significance), bipolar heritability and prevalence (rv-ch73-bipolar-heritability-prevalence) and the autism prevalence figure (rv-ch73-autism-prevalence). Not taught: GWAS genes (ZNF804A, GPR98), opioid GWAS genes, fragile X, amyloid and ACE claims.

objectives: Define a copy number variant and state what chromosomal microarray can and cannot detect.
Name the eight genome-wide significant schizophrenia CNV loci, with deletion or duplication, and the share of cases they explain.
Contrast CNV findings in bipolar disorder with schizophrenia, and state heritability and prevalence figures for bipolar disorder and autism.

scenes.title: Three microarray reports
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three chromosomal microarray (CMA) reports reach a genetics sign-out desk — (1) an adult with schizophrenia: 22q11.2 deletion; (2) an adult with bipolar disorder: 16p11.2 duplication; (3) a child with autism: no reportable copy number change. Question token: “What does each result mean, and what can an array miss?”

cues.text: Three microarray reports arrive. An adult with schizophrenia carries a 22q11.2 deletion. An adult with bipolar disorder carries a 16p11.2 duplication.
And a child with autism has a normal microarray: no copy number change at all.
What does each result mean, and what can a microarray miss?

props.label: What does each mean? What can an array miss?

scenes.title: Copy number variants and the microarray
scenes.altText: Schematic: a chromosome bar with a missing segment (deletion) and a doubled segment (duplication). Card 1: copy number variants (CNVs) are structural changes larger than 1 kb — deletions, duplications, insertions, inversions. Card 2: large (>100 kb), rare (<1% of people) CNVs raise risk for schizophrenia and for neurodevelopmental disorders including autism, intellectual disability, ADHD, developmental delay and epilepsy. Card 3: CMA is the first-tier test for unexplained developmental delay/intellectual disability, autism or multiple congenital anomalies (ISCA consensus 2010): yield 15–20% vs about 3% for a G-banded karyotype. Card 4: truly balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism are generally not detected by arrays.

cues.text: A copy number variant is a structural change larger than one kilobase: a deletion, a duplication, an insertion or an inversion.

Large, rare copy number variants, over one hundred kilobases and carried by fewer than one in a hundred people, raise the risk of schizophrenia and of neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism, intellectual disability and epilepsy.

Chromosomal microarray finds them. A 2010 consensus made it the first-tier test for unexplained developmental delay, autism or multiple congenital anomalies, with a yield of fifteen to twenty percent against about three percent for a karyotype.
Its blind spots: truly balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism are generally not detected, because no DNA is gained or lost overall.

scenes.title: Schizophrenia burden vs bipolar loci
scenes.altText: Left card, schizophrenia (Marshall 2017; 21,094 cases, 20,227 controls): global excess of CNV burden in cases (OR 1.11), still present after excluding known loci; burden enriched for synaptic genes. Eight genome-wide significant loci: losses at 1q21.1, 2p16.3 (NRXN1), 3q29, 15q13.3, distal 16p11.2 and 22q11.2; gains at 7q11.23 and proximal 16p11.2 (1q21.1 also shows gains). Together carried by 1.4% of cases; 22q11.21 deletion has the largest finite odds ratio (about 68). Right card, bipolar disorder (Green 2016; 2,591 cases): studies in general have not found a significant increase in rare CNVs; three schizophrenia loci contribute — 1q21.1 duplication, 3q29 deletion, 16p11.2 duplication — and only 16p11.2 survived multiple-testing correction; very large CNVs (>500 kb, especially deletions >1 Mb) contribute less than in schizophrenia.

cues.text: Schizophrenia first. In a study of more than forty-one thousand people, cases carried a genome-wide excess of copy number variant burden, and it persisted even after the known loci were removed. The extra burden was enriched for synaptic genes.

Eight loci reached genome-wide significance. Most are deletions: 1q21.1, 2p16.3 at NRXN1, 3q29, 15q13.3, distal 16p11.2 and 22q11.2. Two are duplications: 7q11.23 and proximal 16p11.2. Together they are carried by only 1.4 percent of cases.

Bipolar disorder looks different. Studies have generally not found a significant excess of rare copy number variants, and very large ones, especially deletions over one megabase, contribute less than in schizophrenia.
Three schizophrenia loci did show up in bipolar disorder: the 1q21.1 duplication, the 3q29 deletion and the 16p11.2 duplication. Only the 16p11.2 duplication survived correction for multiple testing.

scenes.title: Heritability, prevalence and the hook
scenes.altText: Number card: bipolar disorder — twin-study heritability 60–80% (lower in family and population studies); World Mental Health surveys lifetime prevalence 0.6% bipolar I, 0.4% bipolar II, 2.4% for the whole bipolar spectrum. Autism — heritability about 80% (median 80.8%, five-country cohort of about 2 million children); US surveillance 2020: 27.6 per 1,000 (1 in 36) children aged 8 years, 3.8 times as common in boys. Hook answers: (1) 22q11.2 deletion = the highest-odds schizophrenia locus, but the eight loci explain only 1.4% of cases; (2) 16p11.2 duplication = the one bipolar locus that survived correction; (3) a normal array does not exclude a genetic cause: yield is 15–20%, and balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism are missed.

cues.text: Now the numbers. Bipolar disorder: twin studies put heritability at sixty to eighty percent, with lower family and population estimates. Lifetime prevalence is about 0.6 percent for bipolar one, 0.4 percent for bipolar two, and 2.4 percent for the whole spectrum.

Autism: a five-country cohort of about two million children put heritability near eighty percent. United States surveillance in 2020 found one in thirty-six eight-year-olds, almost four times as many boys as girls.

Back to the hook. The 22q11.2 deletion has the highest odds ratio of the schizophrenia loci, yet all eight loci together explain only 1.4 percent of cases. The 16p11.2 duplication is the bipolar locus that survived correction.
And the child with a normal array still may have a genetic cause: microarray finds an answer in only fifteen to twenty percent, and it misses balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 1 22q11.2 del: top odds, but 8 loci = 1.4% of cases
2 16p11.2 dup: the bipolar locus that passed correction

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Bipolar disorder has the same CNV burden as schizophrenia” (✓ no clear overall excess; fewer very large CNVs; a few shared loci); “A schizophrenia CNV hot spot explains most cases” (✓ the eight loci are carried by 1.4% of cases); “A normal microarray rules out a genetic cause” (✓ yield 15–20%; balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism missed; autism heritability ~80%).

cues.text: Trap one: bipolar disorder carries the same copy number burden as schizophrenia. No: bipolar disorder shows no clear overall excess, only a few shared loci.
Trap two: the schizophrenia hot spots explain most cases. No: all eight loci together are carried by 1.4 percent of cases.
Trap three: a normal microarray rules out a genetic cause. No: the yield is fifteen to twenty percent, and balanced changes and low-level mosaicism are missed.

props.title: ✗ “Bipolar CNV burden = schizophrenia.”
lines: ✓ No clear excess; a few shared loci

scenes.title: Six losses, two gains, three borrowed
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Schizophrenia: SIX LOSSES, TWO GAINS. Bipolar: THREE BORROWED, ONE PASSED.” Tokens: six losses = 1q21.1, 2p16.3, 3q29, 15q13.3, distal 16p11.2, 22q11.2 · two gains = 7q11.23, proximal 16p11.2 · three borrowed = 1q21.1 dup, 3q29 del, 16p11.2 dup · one passed = 16p11.2 dup. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: schizophrenia has six losses and two gains. Bipolar disorder borrowed three of those loci, and only one passed the strict test: the 16p11.2 duplication.

Where it breaks: 1q21.1 shows both deletions and duplications in schizophrenia; the bipolar loci come from one United Kingdom sample and need independent replication; and locus lists change as studies grow.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Schizophrenia: global CNV excess · 8 loci · only 1.4% of cases”, “Bipolar: no clear excess, 16p11.2 dup · Autism ~80% heritable · normal array ≠ not genetic”.

cues.text: Schizophrenia shows a genome-wide excess of rare copy number variants at eight hot spots that together explain under two percent of cases, bipolar disorder shares only a few of those loci without a clear overall excess, and a normal microarray does not rule out a genetic cause in highly heritable autism.

props.label: Schizophrenia: global CNV excess · 8 loci · only 1.4% of cases
Bipolar: few shared loci · Autism ~80% heritable · normal array ≠ not genetic

explanation.what: Plain language: some people are missing, or carry an extra copy of, a stretch of a chromosome. A few such stretches raise the risk of schizophrenia strongly, a handful show up in bipolar disorder, and autism is mostly inherited even though a microarray usually comes back normal. Scientific terms: copy number variant (CNV), deletion (loss), duplication (gain), CNV burden, genome-wide significance, chromosomal microarray (CMA), G-banded karyotype, balanced rearrangement, mosaicism, heritability, lifetime prevalence.
explanation.why: Large, rare CNVs change the dosage of many genes at once, and in schizophrenia the excess burden is enriched for synaptic genes. Because each locus is rare, even strong-acting CNVs explain only a small share of cases, while most inherited risk lies elsewhere.
explanation.measure: Schizophrenia (21,094 cases vs 20,227 controls): global CNV burden OR 1.11; genome-wide loci = losses at 1q21.1, 2p16.3 (NRXN1), 3q29, 15q13.3, distal 16p11.2, 22q11.2 and gains at 7q11.23 and proximal 16p11.2; 1.4% of cases carry one; 22q11.21 deletion OR about 68. Bipolar (2,591 cases): 1q21.1 dup (P = 0.022), 3q29 del (P = 0.03), 16p11.2 dup (P = 2.3 × 10⁻⁴, the only one surviving correction); fewer very large deletions than schizophrenia. Bipolar twin heritability 60–80%; lifetime prevalence BP-I 0.6%, BP-II 0.4%, spectrum 2.4%. Autism heritability about 80%; US 2020 prevalence 27.6 per 1,000 children aged 8. CMA yield 15–20% vs karyotype about 3%.
explanation.differs: Schizophrenia (genome-wide CNV excess, eight loci) vs bipolar disorder (no clear overall excess, three shared loci); deletion vs duplication at the same region (distal vs proximal 16p11.2); CMA (copy number) vs karyotype (balanced rearrangements).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the locus list for schizophrenia, recognise that bipolar disorder does not share the overall CNV excess, identify what a normal microarray cannot exclude, or recall autism heritability of about 80%.

mnemonic.text: Schizophrenia: SIX LOSSES, TWO GAINS. Bipolar: THREE BORROWED, ONE PASSED.
mnemonic.explanation: Six deletion loci and two duplication loci reached genome-wide significance in schizophrenia; bipolar disorder showed three of them, and only the 16p11.2 duplication survived correction.
mnemonic.limitation: 1q21.1 shows both deletions and duplications in schizophrenia; the bipolar loci come from one UK sample and need replication; locus lists change as studies grow.

questions.stem: Which statement about copy number variants (CNVs) in bipolar disorder compared with schizophrenia is correct?

options.text: Bipolar disorder shows no clear overall excess of rare CNVs, but a few schizophrenia loci such as the 16p11.2 duplication contribute
options.rationale: Correct. Studies have generally not found a significant rare-CNV excess in bipolar disorder; the 16p11.2 duplication survived correction.

options.text: Bipolar disorder carries a larger burden of very large deletions than schizophrenia
options.rationale: Incorrect. Very large CNVs, especially deletions over 1 Mb, contribute less in bipolar disorder.

options.text: Bipolar disorder shares all eight schizophrenia loci at genome-wide significance
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only three loci showed evidence, and only one survived correction.

options.text: CNVs play no role at all in bipolar disorder
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 1q21.1 duplication, 3q29 deletion and 16p11.2 duplication showed evidence of contribution.

questions.stem: In the 41,321-subject schizophrenia CNV study, which locus was a duplication (gain) rather than a deletion?

options.rationale: Correct. Gains at 7q11.23 and proximal 16p11.2 reached genome-wide significance.
Incorrect. The 22q11.2 locus is a deletion, with the largest finite odds ratio.
Incorrect. The 3q29 locus is a deletion.
Incorrect. The NRXN1 locus is a deletion.

questions.stem: A child with autism has a normal chromosomal microarray. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: A genetic cause is not excluded: microarray yield is 15–20%, and it misses balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism
options.rationale: Correct. Most tested patients have a normal array, and autism heritability is about 80%.

options.text: Autism in this child must be environmental
options.rationale: Incorrect. A normal array does not exclude genetic causes; autism is highly heritable.

options.text: A G-banded karyotype has a higher diagnostic yield and should replace the array
options.rationale: Incorrect. Karyotype yield is about 3%; microarray is the first-tier test.

options.text: The array would have detected any balanced translocation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Truly balanced rearrangements are generally not detected by arrays.

claims.text: CNV definition; large rare CNVs raise risk for schizophrenia and neurodevelopmental disorders.
CMA first-tier; yield 15–20% vs karyotype about 3%; balanced rearrangements and low-level mosaicism missed.
Schizophrenia global CNV burden OR 1.11; synaptic enrichment; eight loci with direction; 1.4% of cases; 22q11.21 deletion largest finite OR.
Bipolar disorder: no clear overall rare-CNV excess; fewer very large CNVs; 1q21.1 dup, 3q29 del, 16p11.2 dup, only 16p11.2 surviving correction.
Bipolar twin heritability 60–80%; lifetime prevalence BP-I 0.6%, BP-II 0.4%, spectrum 2.4%.
Autism heritability about 80%; US 2020 prevalence 1 in 36 children aged 8; 3.8 times as common in boys.
A normal array does not exclude a genetic cause in autism.
claims.note: Inference from the 15–20% diagnostic yield, array blind spots and about 80% heritability; no source states it in these words.

claims.text: Reviewer heritability “>70%” for bipolar disorder; GWAS genes; East Asian or other-ancestry CNV loci.
“Six losses, two gains, three borrowed, one passed.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 73 Hit 4 lists seven schizophrenia CNV hot spots without direction. Marshall 2017 reports eight genome-wide loci (16p11.2 distal deletion and proximal duplication counted separately): losses at 1q21.1, 2p16.3, 3q29, 15q13.3, distal 16p11.2 and 22q11.2, gains at 7q11.23 and proximal 16p11.2, carried together by only 1.4% of cases. The lesson teaches direction and the 1.4% figure (register flag rv-ch73-scz-cnv-direction).

Ch. 73 Hit 10 and Trap 3 call 1q21.1 dup, 3q29 del and 16p11.2 dup the strongest bipolar CNVs. In Green 2016 only the 16p11.2 duplication (P = 2.3 × 10⁻⁴) survived multiple-testing correction; 1q21.1 (P = 0.022) and 3q29 (P = 0.03) were nominal, and the authors call for independent replication. The lesson teaches this (register flag rv-ch73-bipolar-cnv-significance).

Ch. 73 Hit 10 gives bipolar heritability “>70%” and prevalence “1–2%”. Kerner 2014 gives twin-study heritability of 60–80%, with lower family and population estimates; Merikangas 2011 gives lifetime prevalence 0.6% BP-I and 0.4% BP-II (about 1% combined) and 2.4% for the broader spectrum. The lesson teaches the source figures (register flag rv-ch73-bipolar-heritability-prevalence).

Ch. 73 Hit 12 says autism affects “>1% of children”. US surveillance for 2020 (Maenner 2023) found 27.6 per 1,000 (1 in 36) children aged 8 years, ranging 23.1–44.9 by site; the figure is US-only and depends on case-finding method. The lesson teaches the 2020 US figure with that context (register flag rv-ch73-autism-prevalence).

morphology.note: No karyograms or array plots; results shown as cards.

verification.notes: Seven factual claims checked against Marshall 2017 (results read via a page-fetch tool), Green 2016, Kerner 2014, Merikangas 2011, Bai 2019, Maenner 2023 and Miller 2010; several sources were read as abstracts only. One pending claim (reviewer heritability figure, GWAS genes, other-ancestry loci) is not taught. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
